title: Unlawful order to cull all farmed mink (2020) and the Mink Commission's criticism
description: At a press conference on 4 November 2020 Frederiksen announced that all farmed mink in Denmark, up to 17 million animals according to the BBC, would be culled because a mutated coronavirus variant had been found on farms. Days later it emerged that there was no legal basis for ordering all mink to be culled; Food Minister Mogens Jensen later resigned. DR reported on 18 November 2020 that six ministers in the government's COVID-19 committee had been told on 1 October 2020 that culling all mink would require a change in the law. The Mink Commission, a commission of inquiry that questioned Frederiksen in December 2021, reported on 30 June 2022 that her statements at the press conference were 'objectively grossly misleading' to mink breeders and the public, but that she 'subjectively had no knowledge of or intention' about the missing legal basis, so it did not assess gross negligence; it accepted that she was told only on the evening of 8 November 2020. Its heaviest criticism went to officials, including the Prime Minister's permanent secretary Barbara Bertelsen and national police commissioner Thorkild Fogde, and it found grounds for disciplinary action against ten senior civil servants.
key_facts: 5 July 2022: a majority of the Folketing's scrutiny committee (S, RV, SF, EL) gave Frederiksen and Mogens Jensen a formal reprimand ('næse'); the centre-right opposition parties said it was far from enough (TV 2)
No independent legal assessment that could have led to impeachment (rigsret) was ordered
The Social Liberals demanded an election before 4 October 2022; Frederiksen called one on 5 October for 1 November 2022

title: Deleted text messages from the mink case
description: During the Mink Commission's work it emerged that Frederiksen and her closest advisers had set their phones to delete text messages automatically, for security reasons, so messages exchanged before the November 2020 cull decision were gone. In 2021 the Defence Intelligence Service (FE) and the police concluded that they could not be recovered. In October 2025 Berlingske and B.T. published an internal FE telephone memo from 2021 in which an FE employee suggested another recovery method could be tried; the opposition called an urgent debate (hasteforespørgsel) in the Folketing on 22 October 2025. There Frederiksen said her only wish had been for the messages to be recovered and that 'hardly any process has been examined more than this one', and Justice Minister Peter Hummelgaard said FE had been told on 4 December 2021 that the other method had also been tried. Both rejected the opposition's demand for new investigations (DR).
key_facts: Auto-deletion of text messages on the phones of the Prime Minister and close advisers
2021: FE and police said the messages could not be recovered
22 October 2025: government rejects new inquiries in an urgent parliamentary debate

title: Abolition of the Store Bededag public holiday (2022–2023)
description: On 14 December 2022 Frederiksen's new SVM government proposed abolishing Store Bededag, a holiday observed since the 17th century, from 2024 to raise about DKK 3 billion a year so that defence spending could reach 2% of GDP by 2030 rather than 2033. The plan was opposed by the opposition parties, trade unions and church figures (BBC); a petition to keep the holiday passed 477,000 signatures and some 50,000 people protested outside parliament in early February 2023. Frederiksen said in January 2023: 'I don't think it's a problem to have to work an extra day' (BBC). The Folketing adopted the abolition on 28 February 2023 by 95 votes to 68; according to the BBC there was not enough opposition in parliament to call a referendum. Bishop Marianne Christiansen later described it as a political intervention in the internal affairs of the National Church (folkekirken.dk).
key_facts: Vote of 28 February 2023: 95 (S, V, M, RV) to 68
About 50,000 protesters outside the Folketing in February 2023 (BBC)
October 2026: Frederiksen's third government plans a bill in spring 2027 to reinstate the holiday from 2030

title: Trump cancels state visit after Frederiksen calls Greenland purchase idea 'absurd' (2019)
description: In August 2019 US President Donald Trump confirmed reports that he was interested in buying Greenland, an autonomous territory of the Kingdom of Denmark. Frederiksen, in office for less than two months, described the idea as 'absurd' and said she hoped he was not being serious. On 20 August 2019 Trump cancelled a state visit to Denmark planned for early September at Queen Margrethe II's invitation, saying on Twitter that she had 'no interest in discussing the purchase of Greenland'; the royal house called the cancellation 'definitely a surprise' (BBC).
key_facts: State visit planned for 2 September 2019 cancelled

The dispute returned in 2025–2026; it ended with the Greenland–Denmark–US defence agreement signed on 22 September 2026, which recognises Danish sovereignty and Greenland's right to self-determination

title: Revocation of residence permits of Syrian refugees from the Damascus area (2020–2021)
description: Under Frederiksen's first government Denmark became the first European country to revoke the residence permits of Syrian refugees, on the grounds that the security situation in some parts of Syria, including the Damascus area, had 'improved significantly'. According to The Guardian (April 2021), at least 189 Syrians had been refused renewal of temporary residence since summer 2020 and about 500 people from the Damascus area were being re-examined. The Danish Refugee Council called the rules 'undignified treatment' and noted that neither the UN nor other countries considered Damascus safe for return.
key_facts: At least 189 renewals refused since summer 2020 (The Guardian, 14 April 2021)
Policy criticised by the Danish Refugee Council and human-rights groups

title: Law allowing asylum seekers to be sent to a country outside Europe (2021)
description: In June 2021 the Folketing adopted, 70 votes to 24, the Frederiksen government's bill allowing Denmark to transfer asylum seekers to a partner country outside Europe for their claims to be examined. According to The Guardian (Reuters), the law drew anger from human-rights advocates, the UN and the European Commission, whose spokesperson said external processing of asylum claims 'is not possible under existing EU rules or proposals under the new pact for migration and asylum'. Social Democratic immigration spokesperson Rasmus Stoklund said the government hoped people would stop seeking asylum in Denmark. No partner country had been agreed at the time; Denmark had signed diplomatic agreements with Rwanda in April 2021.
key_facts: Bill L 226 adopted 3 June 2021 (S, V, DF, KF, NB, LA for; SF, RV, EL, ALT against)
No transfers under the law reported; the June 2026 government platform still aims for centres outside Europe

title: Social Democratic support, under her leadership, for the 2016 asylum law allowing seizure of refugees' valuables
description: As leader of the opposition Social Democrats, Frederiksen led her party in supporting the Venstre government's asylum package (bill L 87), adopted on 26 January 2016 by 81 votes to 27. It allowed police to search asylum seekers and their luggage to seize cash and valuables to cover the costs of their stay, delayed family reunification for people with temporary protection from one to three years and tightened the rules for permanent residence. Three Social Democratic MPs voted against. At the UN Human Rights Council's review of Denmark in January 2016, several states criticised the planned seizure of valuables (The Local/AFP).
key_facts: Vote of 26 January 2016: 81 (S, DF, V, LA, KF) to 27; Act No. 102 of 3 February 2016
Three S MPs (Daniel Toft Jakobsen, Mette Gjerskov, Yildiz Akdogan) voted against

title: Danish–Italian open letter calling for a new interpretation of the European Convention on Human Rights (2025)
description: On 22 May 2025, after a meeting in Rome between Frederiksen and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, nine Council of Europe member states, at the initiative of Denmark and Italy, published an open letter calling for 'a new and open-minded conversation about the interpretation of the European Convention on Human Rights', especially on migration; it was also signed by Austria, Belgium, the Czech Republic, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania and Poland. Council of Europe Secretary General Alain Berset replied on 24 May 2025: 'Debate is healthy, but politicising the Court is not. In a society governed by the rule of law, no judicial body should be subject to political pressure.'
key_facts: Letter published 22 May 2025 by nine states (The Local/AFP)
Council of Europe Secretary General: the Court must not face political pressure (Euronews, 24 May 2025)
2 June 2026: Frederiksen said her new government would continue the Danish–Italian initiative
